userStories.title: Follow any playback end to end, and see why the cluster needed more workers
userStories.description: An operator must be able to see exactly where a playback stalled and why the cluster needed more workers, not only that a film is transcoding. Metrics (JS-019) give totals: stalls happened, the queue is deep. This adds one OpenTelemetry trace per playback (PlaySessionId) across the api, stream and worker processes: PlaybackInfo and its decision with reasons; each segment request and where its time went (served from the store, waited on a job, started a job); the job queued, claimed (queue time, which worker) and its ffmpeg runs with their speed; helpers started, and helpers wanted but not started for lack of a free slot; and a failover (lock lost, reap, replacement). The reasons for more workers become metrics too, which autoscaling (JS-057) scales on, so the reason it scaled is visible. Viewers keep seeing in their app that a film is transcoding and why (JS-067).
acceptanceCriteria: One trace per playback session spans the api, stream and worker processes, its context carried in the transcode job row across the Postgres handoff

Given a stalled segment (over 5 s), its trace shows which part took the time: waiting for a free slot, an encode slower than real time, the upload, or reading the store; the stall metric links to the trace (exemplar)
A failover shows the dead worker's span end and the replacement's begin in one trace
Helper decisions are traced and counted: helpers started with the job's speed, and helpers wanted but not started because no slot was free
The demand number and its reasons are JS-164's; a playback's trace shows the same reason for that playback, so why the cluster grew can be read back from either
Log lines carry the trace id (JS-022), so a trace leads to its logs
jellyfin-web's playback info still shows transcoding, its reasons and speed (JS-067), and stays right while helpers run (the viewer's own job may have ended)
Exported over OTLP to any backend, off by default; the dogfood runs a backend and the docs show reading a stall from it
Checked with real processes: a test collector receives a playback's trace from three processes, with a stall and a failover in it
userStories.notes: Needs a design review; the homelab has no tracing backend yet (Tempo suggested). Product owner (2026-11-08): wants to trace everything through the pipeline, see where something stalled and why more workers were needed; placed before P6 (Kubernetes). JS-024 review (UX): Sessions can show the viewer's job as done while helpers encode, and no log line says a helper started.

userStories.title: Logging slice
userStories.description: Consistent, structured logs per role with request and job ids, so an operator can follow one playback.
acceptanceCriteria: Each request and job log line carries ids that link them

An ERROR line means a failure an operator may need to act on. Levels and noise are reviewed against the dogfood, and three cases are settled: a library asset store that nothing has yet been written to is swept as empty and logs no ERROR or WARN (D-069; the media scan's rule for a missing root, invariant 56, is unchanged; whether an asset root lost after assets were stored can still be told and reported is recorded and returns as a brief, not built); a Postgres switchover the worker survives logs no ERROR (BL-067); a failed job that a fresh job replaced is not logged as an unrecovered failure, and docs/running.md says how it is counted (BL-167). The e2e and roles tiers then fail on a level=ERROR line in a scenario that causes no fault; a scenario that causes one names the lines it expects by their reason, not their text.
Each line of a playback carries its play session id and trace id (JS-021), and a helper's start, end and failure say they are a helper's and whose
Metrics beyond the transcode path: HTTP requests by role, route and status with latency, store operations and bytes by store, scan durations and errors

Every figure the docs tell an operator to watch is a series on /metrics, and docs/running.md's table lists every series the endpoint serves, compared once by hand with a live /metrics answer when the task closes, the comparison recorded; no test reads the doc (D-069, superseding D-038's 'by a check').

userStories.title: User management
userStories.description: Create, delete, disable users; change passwords; preferences and configuration.
acceptanceCriteria: POST /Users/New, DELETE /Users/{id}, /Users/{id}/Policy, /Password as Jellyfin 12.4
jellyfin-web's admin user pages work
Login attempts are throttled per user and per client address, and the Policy's lockout fields work as Jellyfin 12.4's do

'admin' joins Route.Access: POST /Users/New, DELETE /Users/{userId}, POST /Users/{userId}/Policy and GET /Auth/Providers declare it; a viewer gets 403 on each and TestAccess asks (named mutant: the guard treating admin as viewer)
GET /Users answers a viewer a list of one, themselves, and an administrator everyone; POST /Users and the password routes are admin-any

Policy says only what is enforced: IsAdministrator, IsDisabled, EnableContentDownloading and the two lockout fields are stored and act; a POST changing any other field from the value GET answers is 400 naming the field and stores nothing; GET's own Policy posted back answers 204

Disabled or deleted, at once: sign-in answers the same 401, in the same time, as a wrong password; forced with real processes, every token of the user answers 401 on the next request through another api process and through stream

The last administrator: forced, two administrators each demote the other through two api processes with both statements held on the users rows until pg_stat_activity shows both waiting, then released: exactly one answers 204, the other 403, and one enabled administrator remains; the same for disable and delete (named mutant: counting administrators before the update, outside its transaction)
Passwords: changing your own needs the current one; an administrator resets another's without it; either revokes the user's other tokens, shown on a second process

A revoked device or disabled user's running stream stops: forced, a direct play of the whole file read slowly when the device is revoked or the user disabled closes within 15 seconds having sent less than the file
LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout stays -1 and a set value is not honoured, as compat/differences.yaml says (D-020); a new or changed password is refused if it is among the commonly guessed ones
userStories.notes: /Configuration moved to JS-116 (2026-11-15). Access criteria from the access model (2026-11-16). Refine with care: a throttle per client address needs a trusted-proxy setting first (behind an ingress every request has its address), and a lockout by user name lets anyone lock a known account out. State what start-up does when the configured administrator was deleted or demoted through the API. D-069: named mutants are shown failing once by hand in the Spec step and recorded in the task's record; no mutant table or script is committed.

userStories.title: Use every GPU and CPU the cluster has
userStories.description: What JS-170 (the first slice: Intel VAAPI/QSV) leaves, under D-047's rule: NVIDIA NVENC and AMD VAAPI workers, hardware decoding for processor-encoded streams, and outputs above 1080 lines. fMP4 can't splice across encoder families (spikes/seam: x264 spliced with NVENC lost half the frames), so each stream keeps one family, and its helpers (JS-024) and failover stay in it. D-047.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building: how a stream's family is chosen among several hardware families and the processor; what a viewer sees when the last worker of their stream's family is lost mid-film (as JS-170 settled it, or briefed); whether a copy and a re-encode share one slot pool; and whether a GPU family re-encodes above 1080 lines, from JS-148's figures (D-021).

NVIDIA NVENC and AMD VAAPI workers detect by a bounded real test of each stage at start, with nothing configured, and choose per job by D-047's rule (the same picture within its bound, 1.2 times real time measured, within twice x264's bytes, then the least processor; the processor otherwise, logged and counted with its reason). A node with no GPU runs exactly as before.

A new stream gets a hardware family when a worker of it has room and the processor otherwise; the family stays in the spec hash; helpers and failover stay in the family; a seek, a restart and a helper's chunk splice in jellyfin-web on each family.
Hardware decoding for processor-encoded streams only where its frames are measured equal to software decoding, per codec and family; otherwise software decoding.
The tone map's curve is the one jellyscale sets in every family; no driver tone map (D-047).
Tested on real hardware in its own tier, chosen explicitly and never skipped: NVENC and AMD VAAPI on a developer machine; jellyfin-web plays, seeks and recovers from a killed GPU worker.
Operators see the family and worker of each stream (Sessions, /metrics, JS-021 traces); the overrides are JS-170's three and no more.
An optional GPU worker pool requests nvidia.com/gpu or the vendor's resource through its device plugin; documented in docs/running.md.
userStories.source: PRODUCT.md phase5-library; rewritten 2026-11-08: the product owner wants every GPU and CPU in the cluster used where possible, priority kept in P5; D-047
userStories.notes: The dogfood cluster has an Intel iGPU on each of its three nodes (gpu.intel.com/i915: 1 allocatable) and the user's Jellyfin requests one; the developer machine has an RTX 4070 Ti and an AMD iGPU. GPU tone mapping (libplacebo or vendor filters) gives frames unlike zscale's, so it splices only within its own family. JS-154: the HD 530 cannot decode HEVC Main 10 or tone map in its video processor; software decode, OpenCL tone map and VAAPI encode reached 1.09x in a quiet pod, at 31 times x264's bytes at the bitrate tried. The UHD 630 nodes were measured by JS-163 and are JS-170's.

userStories.title: Kubernetes example manifests
userStories.description: Example manifests an operator applies with kubectl: deployments per role, readiness and liveness, Postgres (CNPG), configuration as plain files. Split from the Helm chart (JS-142) by the direction review, 2026-11-19: an operator cannot install jellyscale today.
acceptanceCriteria: Example manifests in the repository install jellyscale on a fresh cluster with kubectl alone (`kubectl apply -k` or `-f`), no Helm
Readiness and liveness probes per role

The manifests size CNPG's max_connections from their own configuration: every process's databaseMaxConns plus the direct connections each worker holds (liveness, lease keeper, and one per running scan, segment sweep or asset sweep pass), with headroom; configuration whose sum exceeds it is refused by a check
Each probe states what it depends on: liveness never depends on Postgres or a store, so a database failover restarts no pod; ffmpeg threads follow the pod's CPU limit, not the node's cores
The worker's liveness URL can come from the environment or a Secret, and the manifests never put a password in a process's arguments
docs/running.md says which Postgres connection modes are supported (session; a transaction-mode pooler or pgx exec mode, supported or not, by a check), and the manifests connect that way
A replica whose database stays broken leaves service, and the manifests' grace period and readiness lead match the documented ones
The example manifests declare trustedProxies for their ingress (D-020)

The procedure in docs/running.md for confirming declared proxies, followed against the example manifests' ingress, says what the operator sees and does when no address is counted (every answer 401, no refusal line), and no sentence there denies a log line the server writes (D-025, BL-221)

Workers are their own Deployment, apart from api and stream, and the manifests' check refuses more than one worker or stream replica on a transcode store or library that not every one of them can reach (a ReadWriteOnce volume), naming the key (D-045)
docs/running.md says what every worker must reach (Postgres, each library, the transcode store), and the worker's termination grace matches JS-165's (D-045)
The example manifests declare no transcodeCores and give workers CPU requests equal to limits in whole cores (D-064)
userStories.notes: JS-020 (2026-11-08): each worker holds one Postgres connection for its liveness lock, outside the pool, so a stock Postgres (max_connections 100) is exhausted at about 90 workers, long before its CPU (one primary carried 1600 streams on two cores' worth). Connections are the first wall when autoscaling. User (2026-11-08): plain manifests for kubectl are wanted beside the chart, not Helm only. JS-166 (D-067): its docs/running.md part was not written and is carried by criteria 10 and 11 here and JS-177's 'Sizing workers'. From its record, criterion 11's text covers: every role given the same transcodeStore and its S3 credentials; and that a request equal to the limit may not schedule beside a node's other workloads (the dogfood's worker requests 6 under a limit of 12), which is why a 4K-capable worker wants a whole node. D-069: each 'by a check' in criteria 3, 6 and 10 is met by the application refusing or warning at start with the key named, or by the shipped manifests applied to a real cluster in this task's own run; no test reads the manifest files. A criterion that cannot be met that way returns as a brief when the task starts. D-071: the example worker's CPU limit is one the docs' rules hold for (a 2-CPU limit counts 2.0, under the 4K HDR job's 2.08 share). The example configuration names no `transcodeSlots`; whether that key is removed or capped at the CPUs returns as a brief at Refine.

No ExoPlayer client or AVPlayer client (Swiftfin) has played a jellyscale stream (Findroid and Android TV's direct play send no token on media requests and are not targets, D-026), which the Phase 0 report left open (spikes/README.md, remaining risks 1 and 2), and the decision engine answers direct play to any client whose profile has no fMP4 HLS entry (internal/playback/decide.go). Before more is built on the segment format (JS-054), the owner plays films on real devices against the dogfood, and the lead records what each client asked for and what it played. Web-first stays the plan; this is a check that the format holds.
acceptanceCriteria: The owner plays, against the dogfood, on Jellyfin for Android with its built-in ExoPlayer player (not the web player in its WebView, and with the external player option off) and on Swiftfin with its native AVPlayer player, both read from source as sending their token on every media request (D-030): a direct play, an HEVC or 4K film that transcodes, a seek, an audio switch, a text and an image subtitle. The record names the engine that played each, from the app's setting and the server's log; a run on any other player the app offers proves nothing about the family and is recorded as such (a family left without a run on its engine falls under the next criterion)

An app whose player sends no token is recorded as refused (D-005) and not supported (D-026), never as a failure to chase, and no task comes of it; a player family with no client that sends a token is listed in docs/status.md as not proven (no client that sends a token), not a pass

Each client's PlaybackInfo request and the server's decision are recorded from the dogfood's logs, taken from JS-153's decision line (no titles or paths in the record), with what the viewer saw; for each client, whether its request carries an AudioStreamIndex the viewer did not pick (taken from the item's named track) and which track played when the viewer's saved language is not the file's default (D-034)
Each failure becomes a task in tasks/prd.json, placed before JS-054 when it concerns the segment format
docs/status.md says which clients have played which paths
An HEVC HDR copy and its fallback are played once in a browser with an HEVC decoder (E2E_HEVC=1) and recorded; until then docs/status.md says 'checked with ffmpeg only'
Streamyfin's player entries in compat/clients.yaml are corrected from what the device sends

On each client played: a server address typed with a trailing slash still signs in; whether it asks for the subtitle playlist, and what its viewer sees, is recorded; what its viewer reads when a sign-in is refused by JS-145 (403 with Retry-After, D-020) is recorded in docs/access.md, and no task comes of an app's wording

Whether each device's profile declares Dolby Vision is recorded. On one that does: a profile 5 film and a profile 8.1 film from the dogfood are played, with what PlaybackInfo decided (direct play, copy or re-encode) and what the viewer saw. A profile 5 film re-encoded for a client that declares it becomes a task. If neither device declares it, or the dogfood holds no profile 5 film, docs/status.md says profile 5 on a client that declares Dolby Vision is not proven (D-021)

Each played app's direct-play, HLS, subtitle and download requests seen on the dogfood are compared with what was read from source (D-030): a media request that arrives with no token from an app listed as sending one moves that app to not supported in docs/status.md (D-026), and no task comes of it

For each app played: whether it asked for a Trickplay route, and whether its sign-in screen offered a code (Quick Connect), with what the server answered and what the viewer saw (nothing, a missing preview, an error); an error a viewer sees is brought to the product owner (BL-222), and no route is built in this task

Moonfin on an Android TV device signs in and plays one direct play and one film that transcodes, recorded like the others with the engine that played; if it is not run, docs/status.md says no Android TV app has played; on a film with several subtitle tracks, the subtitle index Moonfin asked for and the track it resolved to are recorded, with its subtitle mode (finding 5, D-038)

userStories.title: Mixed versions are safe: migrations and spec hashes across a rolling upgrade
userStories.description: Every dogfood deploy already runs two versions side by side, but upgrade safety is one line at the end of the plan (JS-058). Migrations run with no lock timeout and no check for migrations a newer version applied (internal/db/db.go), an old worker can compute another spec hash than a new one (ARCHITECTURE.md known departures), and docs/running.md and ARCHITECTURE.md disagree on which role rolls first.
acceptanceCriteria: Migrations take a lock timeout and a version that finds a migration newer than it knows refuses to start with a clear message
A worker of the previous version and one of this version serve the same stream, in a real-process test, without a spec hash disagreement breaking playback (or the job is refused by the older one)
One documented rollout order, the same in docs/running.md and ARCHITECTURE.md, and a test or check that each migration in a release is safe for the previous version's code

With a stream replica of the previous decision version registered and an api replica of the new one, PlaybackInfo offers nothing the old replica would refuse (a real-process test), and docs/running.md no longer requires an order between api and stream

A worker of the previous release is never counted as a partner for a shared play unless it has said it can help: during a rolling upgrade no play is admitted as shared and then left without a helper, in a real-process test (D-061).

Observed first with real processes under a playing film: a migration that takes exclusive locks on two tables a running worker and a stream replica use is applied while they run. The upgrading replica starts (it applies the migration again after a deadlock or lock timeout) or refuses once with a message naming the lock; it never fails to start silently. No viewer request is answered an error. The record says what a stream replica answers from memory if Postgres stops just after its snapshot read was aborted; a gap there returns to the product owner as a brief and is not built here (D-063).
userStories.notes: Before JS-054, which adds encoder families to the spec. The version-gated claim moved to JS-082 (2026-11-12). Extended from the Fable 5.2 blind audit, 2026-11-14. When it starts it is split into migrations (criteria 1, 3, 6) and mixed-version play (2, 4, 5) (D-063).

userStories.title: DOMAINS.md defines the domains; each domain's detail lives with it
userStories.description: DOMAINS.md is 141 KB, with single invariants thousands of words long on one line. Every agent reads it on every task, readers' tools cut its lines short, and it drifts from the code. It becomes the definition of the domains: for each domain its vocabulary, its boundary (what it owns and must not do), and its guarantees as numbered rules of one to three sentences. Each rule's full statement, rationale, measurements, tables, tests and history move whole to one file per domain under docs/domains/, read by tasks that touch that domain. Invariant numbers do not change. Documents and their checks only; no behaviour changes.
acceptanceCriteria: DOMAINS.md is organised by domain: each has its vocabulary, its boundary (owns, must not) and its rules; every invariant belongs to exactly one domain; the preamble says what the file is, that a rule and its section in the domain file bind together, and that a change which bends either updates both in the same change

Every invariant in DOMAINS.md is one to three sentences and at most 600 characters, keeps the number it has today (none renumbered or reused; a new rule takes the next number), and links to its section in its domain file
DOMAINS.md has no line over 600 characters and is under 40 KB in all; no domain file has a line over 1,000 characters
Each domain file under docs/domains/ has one section per rule, headed by the rule's number, holding its full statement, rationale, measurements, tables and the names of its tests
Nothing is lost: a check finds each old invariant's full text under its number in its domain file, and a check lists every old invariant's tests against the new files and fails when one is missing
No guarantee is weakened: a short rule contradicts nothing in its section, and any statement that says less than today's cites a decision id from tasks/decisions.json
Every existing citation still resolves, by a check that fails on a number with no rule: in code, docs/, ARCHITECTURE.md, tasks/prd.json and tasks/decisions.json
Every existing citation still resolves: shown by one search run when the task closes, its output recorded; no committed check reads code, docs/, ARCHITECTURE.md or tasks/ (D-069).

The pointers change in the same change: CLAUDE.md, the role files in .claude/agents/ (the product owner's read list included) and the build workflow's instructions say every agent reads DOMAINS.md, and a task's agents also read the domain file of each domain the task touches

userStories.title: Recommendations from each viewer's own history, with a reason for each
userStories.description: Issue #110 (from:fluster) asked for 'Because you watched...' suggestions. The owner decided (2026-11-12) to build them as the first feature beyond Jellyfin's API: a per-account viewer profile built from watch history on the user's own server, computed by workers and stored in Postgres, with nothing sent outside it, served under the jellyscale namespace (/jellyscale/v1/, PRODUCT.md, #112) that unmodified clients never see. It needs watch history that survives scans (JS-076) and the library's genres, people and similar items (JS-046, JS-049).
acceptanceCriteria: A worker builds and updates each account's viewer profile from that account's watch history only, and nothing leaves the server

GET /jellyscale/v1/recommendations (authenticated as a Jellyfin token) answers suggestions for the signed-in viewer, each with a stated reason ('Because you watched X', a shared genre or person), documented and versioned
No Jellyfin route changes behaviour, and an unmodified Jellyfin client never sees the namespace
A viewer with no history gets a sensible answer (empty or popular in the library), and another account's history never shapes a viewer's suggestions

A viewer in a browser sees their suggestions, each with its reason, with no other app: on a page jellyscale serves (as JS-122's), or where jellyfin-web already shows recommendations if what it asks there is observed on Jellyfin 12.4 first and no Jellyfin route changes behaviour

userStories.description: jellyfin-web has no place to turn on hiding tracks outside a viewer's languages, to name the languages to keep, or to show all tracks (JS-118). A small page jellyscale serves, linked from jellyfin-web's user menu, gives a browser-only viewer the same switches through the /jellyscale/v1/ settings JS-118 adds.
acceptanceCriteria: A signed-in viewer reaches the page from jellyfin-web's user menu and sees their two opt-ins, their kept languages and 'show all tracks' as saved

Turning an opt-in on with no default language set asks for one first; the page saves through the /jellyscale/v1/ track-preferences route (JS-118), and the next PlaybackInfo in jellyfin-web reflects it

A viewer whose audio language is saved and whose PlayDefaultAudioTrack is on is told on the page that a film whose default track is in another language still starts in that track (Jellyfin's rule, and its default for every new user), and can turn it off there with one switch, saved through PATCH /jellyscale/v1/users/configuration (JS-123); the next PlaybackInfo in jellyfin-web then names the track in their language
A viewer changes only their own settings; another viewer's are untouched, and an unsigned request is refused
The page works at phone width and in light and dark, with no route outside /jellyscale/v1/ and no change to jellyfin-web's files
userStories.notes: Owner, 2026-11-15: a page, after the track-language batch. Moved up (D-028): the settings are built and no browser viewer can reach them. 2026-11-17 (JS-121's UX review): PlayDefaultAudioTrack defaults to true, so a viewer who only saves a language keeps hearing a film's flagged track, usually its original; the page says so and offers the switch.

userStories.title: A user id in a request names the caller, or the request is refused
userStories.description: About twenty routes take a user id, in the path of the aliases jellyfin-web calls or in a userId query, and ignore it: the answer is the caller's data whatever the id says (routes.go:121, items.go:67). Nothing leaks, but an administrator who asks for another user's list is given their own under the other's name, and no test would notice a handler that started to honour the id without a check. Two handlers that do honour it carry two hand-written copies of the check, in two orders (sessions.go:346-372, user_configuration.go:160-175). This task makes one rule, in one place, before any handler runs.
acceptanceCriteria: Observed first: compat/captures/user-scope-12.4.md and .json record, from a real Jellyfin 12.4 with an administrator and two non-administrators, for every route in compat/endpoints.yaml: the status, and whose data came back, when a non-administrator names the other non-administrator (in the path, and as userId in the query), names an id that is no user, names a malformed id, and when the administrator names a non-administrator. It also records what POST /Items/{itemId}/PlaybackInfo does with a UserId in its body and GET /Sessions with controllableByUserId

Route has Users: 'own' (the default) or 'admin-any'. 'admin-any' is exactly GET /Users/{userId}, POST /Users/Configuration, POST /Users/{userId}/Configuration and POST /UserItems/{itemId}/UserData. --print-routes writes user: for every route that is not 'anyone', and docs/access.md's table is held to it

One guard, before the handler: on every 'viewer' route, a user id in the {userId} path segment, the userId query, the controllableByUserId query or PlaybackInfo's body that is not the caller's answers 403 when the route is 'own', whoever asks, administrators included. Nothing is read or written for the other user. The caller's own id, dashed or compact, in any case, answers as with no id

On an 'admin-any' route one helper decides: a non-administrator naming another user gets 403 before any lookup, whether the id is a user or not; an administrator naming a user acts on that user; an administrator naming nobody known gets 404; a malformed id gets 400. sessions.go and user_configuration.go use the helper and hold no copy

TestAccess asks every 'viewer' route with viewer A's token and viewer B's id, in the path where the route has one and as userId in the query on every route: 403 on all of them. With the administrator's token and B's id: 403 on every 'own' route, and B's record on the four 'admin-any' routes. After the whole sweep B's rows in users, user_item_data, display_preferences and sessions are byte for byte what they were
An 'anyone' route ignores a user id: POST /Users/AuthenticateByName?userId={B} signs A in

Named mutants, each failing every run: the guard reads the path and not the query; the guard lets an administrator through on an 'own' route; the helper looks the user up before it refuses a non-administrator

The one case of JS-116's captured replay that changes is named in the pull request: a non-administrator naming an id that is no user on the Configuration routes got 404 as on Jellyfin and now gets 403, so that the answer no longer says whether the id is a user. Every other case passes unchanged
jellyfin-web still works: the e2e tier passes unchanged (it sends its own id everywhere), and the differential tier passes with no new entry, since its one user names itself

DOMAINS.md invariant 49 and the routes.go comment 'These act on the caller whatever userId says' say the new rule. docs/access.md lists, under 'Stricter than Jellyfin', that an administrator is served another user's view on four routes only, with the capture entry that shows Jellyfin serving it everywhere
userStories.notes: Changed answers, to list in the pull request: a request naming another user's id got 200 with the caller's data and now gets 403; the Configuration 404 above. Neither is visible to a viewer using a client, which always sends its own id.Tests make their second user by SQL, as user_configuration_integration_test.go does; no seeding route is added. Jellyfin's rule is RequestHelpers.GetUserId (Jellyfin.Api/Helpers/RequestHelpers.cs:67-81 at v12.4). Owner's decisions (2026-11-16, on Fable 5.2's access model, .results/access-model-fable-2026-11-16.md): pictures by id open to whoever holds the id, by name need a token; per-library access right after JS-033; a revoked or disabled user's running stream stops within 15 s; a viewer sees no other viewer's name; an administrator manages accounts but never browses, plays or reports as another user; a Policy field jellyscale does not enforce is refused when changed (400); 'may download' is honoured; operator keys are never users; no issue is filed on Findroid for now. D-069: named mutants are shown failing once by hand in the Spec step and recorded in the task's record; no mutant table or script is committed.

userStories.title: A re-encode's x264 preset is part of its spec, and its price follows the preset
userStories.description: Every x264 re-encode uses -preset veryfast (internal/transcode/ffmpeg.go, at both x264 sites). spikes/picture-quality measured faster at +2.5 VMAF on the mean and +3.5 to +5 on the worst frames for 1.2 to 1.6 times the CPU, and medium +0.5 more for 2.2 times. The owner decided (2026-11-19) that operators choose the preset, trading picture against the compute they pay for, with faster the default (JS-136). This task builds what that needs underneath: the spec carries the preset, so every worker that encodes a stream uses the same one (segments of two presets under one init segment fail in Chromium with PIPELINE_ERROR_DECODE, spikes/picture-quality), and Spec.Cost prices each preset from a film measured through a worker, so a worker admits as many jobs as it can keep at real time. The spike also found today's 0.8 cores for a 1080p job low for a hard film (1.36 CPU s per s at veryfast, pinned, unverified basis); this task measures it properly.
acceptanceCriteria: Spec has a preset, one of superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow; it is part of Spec.Hash, so two specs that differ only in it have different hashes, and a spec stored before the field existed reads as veryfast and keeps its hash, so its stored segments are still served

The preset travels in the playlist and segment URLs as the spec's other fields do, so a request answered by any replica rebuilds the same spec and hash whatever that replica would choose; a test asks one stream's playlist and segments of two api replicas and finds one hash

A worker encodes with the spec's preset, never a setting of its own: a test reads the arguments of a re-encode and of an H.264 copy's fallback (recodeArgs) for two presets and finds each spec's preset in each; the HEVC and AV1 fallbacks keep their own presets and say so in docs/transcoding.md

In a rolling upgrade a worker from before this task never takes a job whose preset is not veryfast (it would encode veryfast under that spec's hash, which Chromium cannot decode after the init segment): a mixed-fleet test with a pinned release-before worker, as JS-030's, gives it a faster job and finds it made by a new worker, while veryfast jobs are still shared by both
A test with real segments: a store holding a stream's segments at one preset never serves them for a spec of another preset; the second spec's job encodes its own

A measurement test, run as the AV1 rows are, logs for each of superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow, from a 1080p and a 4K real-film source, SDR and tone mapped, through a worker's own command, on Ubuntu 24.04's ffmpeg 6.1 and on ffmpeg 9: CPU seconds per second of film, and the time to the first segment and to the fourth on 2 and 4 CPUs; docs/transcoding.md records the figures with the machine and the command

Spec.Cost has a row per preset, SDR and tone mapped, 1080p and 4K, in cores of the reference machine docs/transcoding.md names (JS-161), each at or above its measured figure with the margin docs/transcoding.md gives today; the HEVC fallback's x265Extra and the AV1 fallback's rows do not follow the x264 preset; if veryfast's rows are found low and raised, the pull request states, per row, viewers per worker before and after and what the next viewer on a full worker then sees, and the owner approves those numbers before it merges
With real processes: a worker given jobs whose costs add up to its measured capacity (JS-161), at faster and at medium, keeps each at 1.2 times real time or more without a helper
No viewer-visible change while every spec is veryfast: the transcode, seek and helper e2e scenarios pass as before
userStories.notes: Bump OutputVersion only if the arguments of a veryfast spec change; a spec read from before the field must keep its hash (invariant: stored segments of a spec are its output).

userStories.title: Operators choose the x264 preset, faster by default
userStories.description: The owner (2026-11-19): operators choose the preset, deciding how much picture they give up for the compute they pay for, and faster is the default unless they choose another. JS-135 put the preset in the spec and priced it; this task adds the setting, makes faster the default and shows a viewer gains picture without losing a quick start.
acceptanceCriteria: A config key transcodePreset accepts superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow; left out it is faster; any other value stops the start of every role with an error naming the key and the accepted values

userStories.title: An operator and an autoscaler can read that encoding is falling behind, and why
userStories.description: docs/running.md calls jellyscale_transcode_queue_cores the signal to scale workers on, but a play with no free cores is refused, not queued, and a re-encode running under real time is not queued either, so on the dogfood's stalled plays (2026-11-20) that signal read nothing. This task adds one cluster-wide number for demand beyond what the workers hold, with its reason, pulled forward from JS-021 criterion 5. PRODUCT.md: the cluster can grow and shrink with demand by itself; a heavy film uses the whole cluster's processors. D-045.
acceptanceCriteria: Observed first with real processes and recorded: what jellyscale_transcode_queue_cores reads while (a) a watched re-encode runs under real time with no helper possible and (b) a play is refused for lack of free cores. If it reads 0 in both, docs/running.md no longer calls it the signal to scale on. Amended by D-048: JS-162 read 0 at one snapshot of each stalling run (case a, once per run); case b is still unobserved.

A gauge on /metrics gives, in cores and for the whole cluster, the demand the workers do not hold, by reason: jobs queued; helpers wanted by a watched job under 1.2 times real time and not started for lack of room; plays refused for lack of free cores within a stated recent window, and, as its own reason, plays refused because the cores are held by a helper another viewer's film needs (JS-161 criterion 11, D-050). Every worker reports the same number, as queue_cores does Whichever replica refuses, a play refused for a held film is logged and counted with the held-film reason, never as cores short or busy (JS-161 minor, D-061).

Each reason is above zero within 15 seconds of its condition starting and back to zero within a stated time of its ending, so an autoscaler both grows and shrinks on it; checked with two real workers for each reason

A second gauge gives, for the whole cluster and in reference cores, the dearest job a new viewer would be admitted for now, by JS-161's rule (one worker or shared). Cores held by a helper of a watched job its own worker does not hold at 1.2 times real time alone are not free; cores held by any other helper are (JS-161 criterion 11). It falls within 15 seconds of a play starting and rises within a stated time of its ending, checked with two real workers, a viewer's job and a helper. An operator or an autoscaler keeps it above the dearest job they want to start without a wait, so no viewer has to be refused or stall to trigger growth. (D-048)
Not counted as demand: a job no viewer watches, a paused job, a copy reading at its own rate, and helpers when transcodeHelpers is off; docs/running.md says which slowness more workers cannot fix
The only label is the reason: never a job, film, account or device

docs/running.md's metric table and docs/transcoding.md describe both gauges with an example alert and an example scaling query; BL-005's missing reason is readable here. Amended by D-048: the example scaling query is on the room gauge, the example alert on the demand gauge; docs/running.md no longer calls `jellyscale_transcode_queue_cores` the signal to scale on, and says why.
No viewer-visible change
userStories.source: owner direction 2026-11-21; JS-021 criterion 5; D-045; D-048
userStories.notes: ux: true (operators). If JS-161 changes what a refusal for cores means, this counts JS-161's.

userStories.title: A worker removed while films play costs no viewer a stall
userStories.description: An autoscaler removes workers without knowing which are busy, and a rolling upgrade stops every one. docs/transcoding.md says a worker that stops gracefully and is replaced within six seconds is not noticed; whether that holds for a worker that is removed and not replaced, with other workers already running, is unverified. PRODUCT.md: failures are invisible; the cluster can grow and shrink with demand by itself. D-045.
acceptanceCriteria: Observed first, with real processes and jellyfin-web: a worker holding a watched re-encode, a watched copy, a helper and a subtitle extraction gets SIGTERM while another worker has room and no new worker starts. Recorded: what each viewer sees and the longest segment wait. If every criterion below already holds, only the checks and the docs land
From the signal the stopping worker claims no new job
With room on another worker: no segment request over 5 seconds, no dialog, the resume position kept; repeated 10 times in e2e with none failing
With no room on any other worker: what the viewer sees is measured and brought to the product owner as a brief before anything is built for it; it is never a stall without a reason
An interrupted extraction is taken up by another worker and no subtitle request is refused for it
The job's end is counted as interrupted and the log says the worker was stopping
docs/running.md gives the worker's termination grace and what it bounds
No start of play or seek is slower: time to first segment measured before and after

userStories.title: Workers are added before the room for one more film is gone, and when encoding falls behind; removed when idle, by the cluster's own autoscaler
userStories.description: The owner (2026-11-21): scale workers up as soon as encoding falls behind. Kubernetes' autoscaler does the scaling from JS-164's number; jellyscale never creates or removes a pod, and a cluster without an autoscaler runs as before. The example manifests (JS-056) carry it as an option. Replaces 'KEDA autoscaling'. D-045. D-048: spare room first, falling behind and refusals as the backstop and the readable reason.
acceptanceCriteria: The example manifests ship an optional autoscaler for the worker Deployment on JS-164's two gauges; leaving it out changes nothing else. Which autoscaler (the built-in one with a metrics adapter, or KEDA) is chosen by what an operator must run beside it, and docs/running.md states that cost (D-048)

On a real cluster, one worker and a play that falls behind or is refused: a second worker is ready and the film reaches real time; the time from demand to a ready worker, and what the triggering viewer saw meanwhile, are measured and recorded. Amended by D-048: this is the backstop, measured with the target at zero.

By default the example keeps room for one more job of a size the operator states in cores (the example's value is the dearest re-encode in the price table); a worker is added when the room gauge falls below it. A test on a real cluster shows a second viewer starting with no refusal and no stall while the cluster grows. docs/running.md states the cost (one worker's reservation idle at all times) and how to set the target to zero and scale on falling behind alone. (D-048: the first trigger)

After a stated idle time workers are removed down to the minimum, and no watched job stalls over 5 seconds (JS-165); demand that comes and goes changes the worker count no more than a stated number of times
The maximum worker replicas stay within the Postgres connection budget (one liveness connection per worker on top of the pools), refused by the manifests' check otherwise
Each scale-up can be read back with its reason from JS-164's number

Run on the dogfood for 14 days once the owner approves each homelab change; recorded, counts only: scale events by reason, refusals for lack of cores, stalls. Amended by D-048: also records the time the room was below target, and scale-ups by trigger (room, falling behind, refusal).
docs/running.md documents it; docs/transcoding.md no longer says an autoscaler is not built; docs/status.md is updated

userStories.title: Measure whether a GPU re-encode can show the picture the processor makes, in jellyscale's own image
userStories.description: JS-163 answered BL-040's rule in Jellyfin's image with jellyfin-ffmpeg: 4 to 5 times real time, bytes within the bound on two dark scenes, and no GPU tone map matching today's picture. This task measures what a build would rest on. No viewer-visible change. D-047.
acceptanceCriteria: In jellyscale's own image: what it must gain for 10-bit HEVC decode, a GPU tone map with a set curve, subtitle drawing and H.264 encode on an Intel UHD 630 (packages, the image's size before and after), and JS-163's all-hardware and OpenCL rows repeated with it on both nodes, three runs each, in temporary pods of the same kind (own namespace, device plugin, deleted after).

Tone map: the settings tried to bring a GPU tone map whose curve jellyscale sets to the processor path's picture, on a dark, a detailed and a bright high-motion scene from at least two films; for each, brightness above black and SSIM against the processor path, against the bound (within 5% or one code value, whichever is more; at or above 0.99), with one frame of each kept for the brief. The driver video-processor tone maps are not candidates (D-047).

The reverse, priced: the processor path with the curve the GPU tone map and jellyfin-ffmpeg's processor tone map share, its speed on the three nodes' processors and what the image would need (JS-163: 1.98x, 1.40x and 0.97x against 1.36x, 1.06x and 0.85x).

Bytes: the hardware encoder in its quality-targeted modes against x264 veryfast with the worker's 4-second keyframes, on the three scenes, at equal SSIM and by one second measure that rewards what SSIM does not (VMAF, or named otherwise).

On the candidate path (GPU decode, the tone map with a set curve, GPU encode), not the video-processor one: how many jobs at once hold 1.2 times real time each on one node, the processor and the memory each takes, up to the count that fails.
The same row while the node's other GPU user is working, if the owner approves a way to make it work; otherwise marked unverified in the record.
The colour tags written in the bitstream are read as BT.709 by Chromium: a segment played in jellyfin-web, checked on the pixels.
A restart, a seek and a helper's chunk made on the two nodes' GPUs splice in jellyfin-web, as spikes/seam showed for one family.
Recorded in docs/transcoding.md with machine and command, no film title, path or host name; the figures come to the product owner as a brief, every option priced, keeping today's picture among them.
No viewer-visible change, and nothing in the media namespace touched.

userStories.title: A worker finds its Intel GPU by itself and uses it for the re-encodes it does right; the operator sets nothing
userStories.description: The first hardware slice (BL-040): one family, Intel VAAPI/QSV, on GPUs that do the whole job. The worker detects, chooses by D-047's rule and falls back to the processor; operators may turn it off, never need to tune it. NVIDIA, AMD, hardware decode for processor-encoded streams and outputs above 1080 lines stay in JS-054. PRODUCT.md: any film plays, and plays well; play starts in seconds and keeps up; operators want the server to be something they set up once and then mostly forget. D-047.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building: how a family is chosen for a stream; helpers and failover within the family; what a viewer sees when the last worker of their stream's family is lost mid-film (playing on is the goal; anything else is measured and briefed to the product owner before it is built, never a stall or a stop without a reason); how a hardware job is priced against a worker's capacity (JS-161); and whether the task splits (detection and choice; placement and failover).

With nothing configured, a worker tests at start each stage it would use (10-bit HEVC decode, the tone map, subtitle drawing, encode) by a bounded real run, not from the ffmpeg build's list or the device's presence; the bound is in docs/running.md; the result for each stage is logged with its reason and is on /metrics. A node with no GPU, or with none given to the pod, runs exactly as before and logs no error.

A job takes a hardware path only when, on that worker, the path's picture is within JS-169's bound of the processor path's, it measured at or above 1.2 times real time for that kind of job, and its encoder is within twice x264's bytes at equal quality in a quality-targeted mode; otherwise that job is made on the processor there. Checked with a negative case: a worker whose GPU fails a stage (the HD 530 itself in the hardware tier, cannot decode 10-bit HEVC) makes the 4K HDR re-encode on the processor and says why, once, in the log and on /metrics.

The tone map's curve is the one jellyscale sets, in every family; no driver video-processor tone map is used by any path or override. A film's re-encode on a GPU worker and on a processor worker, compared frame for frame on three scenes, is within the bound.

A new stream gets the hardware family when a worker of it has room and the processor otherwise; the family stays in the spec hash; helpers and failover stay in the family. With two UHD 630 workers, in jellyfin-web: a seek, a helper's chunk and a killed GPU worker each splice, no segment request over 5 seconds, no dialog, the position kept; 10 of 10.

Operators may set per worker, and only these: hardware off (default auto), the device, the most hardware jobs at once. An override the hardware cannot honour is refused at start with its reason. docs/running.md says none is needed.

Operators see the family and the worker serving each stream (Sessions, /metrics, the JS-153 decision line); every fall back to the processor is logged with its reason and counted by reason; no label names a job, film, account or device.
Tested on real hardware in its own tier, chosen explicitly and never skipped: the dogfood cluster's UHD 630s.

On the dogfood, each homelab change approved by the owner first (the GPU through the device plugin, no privileged container): a 4K HDR re-encode with and without a burned-in image subtitle plays 10 minutes with a seek at speed 1.0 or above after the first 30 seconds; as many at once on one GPU as JS-169 measured to hold 1.2 times real time each do so; recorded with ids and counts only.

docs/running.md (an optional GPU worker pool and its request), docs/transcoding.md and docs/status.md are updated; DOMAINS.md invariants 23 and 53 are amended citing D-047 where the tone map's filter or the family rule changes.

userStories.title: A worker that starts or restarts does not stall its first heavy film
userStories.description: JS-177 learns a worker's capacity from the jobs it runs, but every start and restart begins at the processors again and overstates the worker until it converges, so the first heavy play after each pod start or rolling upgrade runs under real time. D-066: keep the learned figure in Postgres by hardware class as a start only, and take JS-177's criterion 5, so a newly started pair carries a heavy film.
acceptanceCriteria: An idle worker helps. A watched re-encode under 1.2x, on a worker whose learned capacity is below the job's price, becomes a shared play. A helper is claimed on a worker with 0.65 of the price free, and the viewer returns to real time within JS-168's bound. Checked with two newly started, undeclared workers throttled to the i5-6500's speed.

The learned figure is kept in Postgres by hardware class (CPU model and the processors the process may use), naming no host, pod, film or viewer. A worker that finds one registers at once with it, and D-062's 9 tests pass unamended. Its source reads `remembered` in the log and on `/metrics`.
With real processes: a converged throttled worker is stopped and started. The first 4K HDR play after is refused within seconds with its reason, or admitted shared, as before the stop.

The kept figure is a start only. The worker's own jobs move it by JS-177's rules, both ways and within JS-177's stated times, and it never exceeds `transcodeCores`. The record also states what a timed rise returns the figure to once one is kept, and what the viewer of a play admitted then gets; a kept figure that still admits a play above it by time alone returns as a brief before Spec (D-072).
It is kept while a worker of its class has run in the last 30 days. Every worker starting at once is safe (invariant 2), and a worker of the release before is unharmed.
With nothing kept, the worker starts from its processors. `docs/running.md` says what the first heavy play then gets, for how long, and that an optional ceiling avoids it.
Docs and DOMAINS.md are updated, with the cost stated: one row per class, written at most once a minute on a move of 5% or more.

After it merges, the lead offers the owner dropping the 4-core worker's declared figure, with the dogfood's counters since JS-177 was deployed. The 12-thread worker keeps its ceiling while its CPU request is below its limit, as 'Sizing workers' advises for a shared host (D-072).
userStories.notes: ux: true. Moves to directly after JS-177 on: the dogfood, undeclared, showing a heavy play under 1.0x within 5 minutes of a worker start; or the no_room slow-job reason counted while another worker had 0.65 of the price free. D-073: directly before JS-056. Refine says whether criterion 1 is already what JS-177 built (docs/transcoding.md, 'The first viewer, and a restart', third row); if so it stays a check and adds no build. If the unhelped trigger fires first, criterion 1 alone is split out and built at once. The first trigger can fire only if the owner drops a figure.
